hints: Focus on what DNA polymerase actually does at the replication fork: does it make new nucleotides from scratch, or does it join together free nucleotides that are already there?
Remember the two different bond types in DNA: the strong bonds along each strand in the sugar-phosphate backbone versus the weak bonds holding the two strands together between bases.
walkthrough:
**Picture DNA polymerase at work**

Think of replication like building a new train track alongside the old one. Free DNA nucleotides line up by base pairing, and DNA polymerase is the worker that locks them permanently into the new strand.

It does not make the nucleotides, it joins them together.

**Name the correct bond**

Each new nucleotide must be linked to the previous one to build a continuous strand. DNA polymerase catalyses formation of phosphodiester bonds between the deoxyribose sugar of one nucleotide and the phosphate of the next.

This completes the strong sugar-phosphate backbone.

**Rule out the other bond types**

Complementary bases across the two strands (A to T, C to G) are held by hydrogen bonds, not by the polymerase. And glycosidic bonds are inside a single nucleotide, joining base to pentose sugar, so they are not formed between base pairs.

options.A: False. Free DNA nucleotides are already present in the nucleus. DNA polymerase joins them together, it does not produce them by condensation.
options.B: False. Aligning RNA nucleotides on a DNA template is transcription, carried out by RNA polymerase, not DNA polymerase.
options.C: Correct. DNA polymerase forms phosphodiester bonds between adjacent nucleotides to build the continuous sugar-phosphate backbone of the new strand.
options.D: False. Complementary base pairs are held by hydrogen bonds, and glycosidic bonds join a base to its own sugar within one nucleotide, not between strands.
